Did hiring loads of gamers not work out ? The Federal Aviation Administration is now spending north of $875 million to deploy an AI-powered air traffic control tool, the Wall Street Journal reports .

The system, called SMART — short for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — automatically analyzes factors like airline schedules, weather patterns, and airport runway capacity to help streamline operations and point out any potential conflicts before they occur, according to an official release cited in the reporting.

It’s set to have a huge role. As the WSJ puts it, “when fully rolled out across US airspace, the software is supposed to act as something like the brains of the nation’s air-traffic control system.”

And no pressure to this potentially trailblazing experiment in AI in air traffic operations: it’s first being used in Washington, DC, one of the busiest stretches of airspace in the nation, as soon as Monday.

The rollout of the AI system is the latest step the Trump administration has taken to revamp air traffic control systems, which have been under constant scrutiny after a series of deadly, high profile aviation incidents at the beginning of his term. One of the main issues in the spotlight has been chronic shortage of properly trained air traffic controllers — a problem that precedes Trump’s presidency, to be fair.

US transportation secretary Sean Duffy first teased the FAA’s interest in deploying SMART in April. Back then, he estimated that the government would spend $12 billion on the system, claiming it could help air traffic controllers plan flights weeks in advance.

“This software will say, ‘well, listen, we can see this 45 days out. Let’s move some of those flights a little bit later, or five, seven, 10 minutes earlier, and we can resolve the issue. And so then you are not delayed,'” Duffy said in an interview with CBS News .

The firm behind it, Air Space Intelligence, was awarded a $875 million, 12-year government contract earlier this year, according to the new reporting. Some aviation industry figures find the scale of its rollout to be much smaller to what they were hoping, it noted.

Politico fleshes out the situation a bit more. According to its coverage , FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that the goal is to expand SMART after a 90-day testing period. But until the announcement about its limited scale, many in the industry were panicking about how extensively the AI would be weaved into everyday air traffic operations.

Three airline officials claimed that the industry was baffled about how the tool would even work. Some feared that the AI would create chaos by recommending more flights be cancelled or rescheduled to avoid potential bottlenecks.

“We’ve been requesting and… talking to [FAA] and saying, ‘Let’s narrow the scope of this. Start, crawl, walk, run.’ And I think ultimately that’s what they decided to do,” one anonymously quoted airline industry official told Politico .

Do we have airliners to thank for walking the FAA back from the “full-send AI” brink, then? As their concerns mounted, the FAA held a series of meetings to answer their questions and assuage their concerns, with perhaps scaling back the AI rollout being one of its concessions. The agency also assured that the AI wouldn’t be directly integrated into day-to-day air traffic management, per Politico . Instead, the tool will be used to generate alternative routing options when air traffic is backed up.

These promises have seemingly now won over key factions of the industry.

“We’re just in the initial stages, but it’s one of the most exciting and bold initiatives taken on by the FAA in decades,” Airlines for America, a trade group representing major airliners, said in a statement.

Well, we hate to burst anyone’s bubble, but a new piece from Politico makes it sure sound like that Congress is completely stumped by how to tackle AI, with over a dozen lawmakers and congressional aides venting to the newspaper about the lack of urgency on the Hill over regulating the tech. Many questioned whether elected representatives fully grasp, or are even capable of grasping, the technology they’re dealing with.

“There is a percentage of my colleagues who are still trying to spell AI,” representative Sam Liccardo (D-CA) told Politico . “We need to dramatically increase the base knowledge of Congress if we’re going to legislate meaningfully,” he added. “And I know that is not going to happen overnight.”

Liccardo likely isn’t exaggerating. Last year, a minor brouhaha erupted over Trump’s secretary of education Linda McMahon repeatedly pronouncing AI as “A1” — yes, like the steak sauce — while bloviating about how important chatbots were in the classroom.

There seems to be a growing consensus on the Hill that there needs to be more substantive AI regulation. These concerns were catalyzed this week after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job at the company, and in a post that went mega viral, warned that AI companies were “gambling with our lives” by building powerful AI models that they knew could destroy humanity.

But no one, it seems, can agree on what that regulation should look like, while many are content to pass the buck on the issue.

Politico points out how senator Ted Cruz (R-TX), who serves as senate commerce chair, endorsed passing legislation to prevent “catastrophic risk” after the Anthropic researcher’s warnings, and pointed to a bipartisan AI bill touted by senate majority leader John Thune (R-SD) and senator Amy Klobuchar (D-MI) that’s supposed to lay out more concrete regulations. But neither senator has said when they plan to actually introduce the bill, and requests for comments to their offices have gone unanswered or were met with a vague statement.

Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and other progressives, meanwhile, are advocating for a ban on developing an AI superintelligence — a technology that, while posing clear existential risks, we don’t know is even possible to build yet.

So is someone in power going to actually do something about regulating AI? It’s probably not a good sign when the actual lawmakers running this country are asking themselves the same question, too.

“You cannot just put your head in the sand on AI and say, ‘I hope it works out.’ You can’t just go in and say, ‘Government’s got the solution — they’re just going to ban it all.’ That’s just not going to work,'” representative Chip Roy (R-TX), a conservative who’s on his way out of office, told Politico . “We’re going to have to be thoughtful as leaders and actually have some friggin’ leadership.”

A blistering new article by education policy writer and cognitive scientist Benjamin Riley took a look under the hood of Alpha School, a private K-12 school company in the US which boasts an AI-based teaching model , among other highly dubious features.

To make the grade, high school students are required to pass an eight-week “bootcamp.” After being invited to follow social media accounts of other students at Alpha School, Riley observed a process more akin to hazing than high school orientation, as the private company made its prospective pupils jump through increasingly degrading hoops to secure their spot on the roster.

For example, students in the bootcamp are required to start a brand-new account on X-formerly-Twitter, for which they’re required to get a minimum of 100 organic followers, pay for X Premium, and post an unknown number of replies to “bigger accounts with real substance,” as one student explained.

“‘Great post’ replies don’t count,” the anonymous student posted in a screenshot shared by Riley. “Buying followers or spamming = automatic fail.”

But forced social media assignments are just the beginning. It isn’t clear what educational purpose this particular trial was supposed to serve, or what the penalty would be for students who fail the heart rate challenge, or the boot camp overall. “I ended up averaging 87bpm,” the student continued, evidently just barely making the grade. “Barely made the cutoff by one single beat, and my hands were shaking the entire rest of the afternoon.”

Talking to an AI chatbot can feel like confiding in a mirror, a private exchange equivalent to brainstorming in a Word document. Yet when it comes to the most popular AI chatbots, that mirror is really one-way glass — and you might be shocked to learn how many different people can watch from the other side.

Since the rise of easily accessible AI chatbots, untold millions of people have happily fed AI models their deepest, darkest secrets. According to a recent survey conducted by browser company DuckDuckGo and flagged by CNET , a full third of all AI users admit to having told their chatbots a secret they wouldn’t tell the “trusted people” in their lives.

There’s a grim irony there, because by telling an AI chatbot those closely guarded secrets, you may inadvertently be sharing intimate details with tech companies, police departments, lawyers, and even your boss. That’s according to new reporting by the Washington Post , which notes that there have been a dozen court cases where chatbot transcripts were cited in the public record over the last two years.

Even if your transcripts don’t end up in the hands of Johnny Law, they can easily be obtained by your boss, assuming you’re using a company-provided AI service. And of course, there’s no telling how long AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic might hold onto details of your conversations, as WaPo notes numerous scenarios in which they may be required to hold onto your chatlogs by law.

There’s also the grim possibility of leaks from the AI companies themselves. In July, it was revealed that a whole trove of chats with Anthropic’s chatbot Claude had been exposed to the open web — and not for the first time .

“Unless you are having a chat with a service that has a temporary chat or, basically, an incognito version… [and] you’re also having it within a browser that’s not tracking you, the answer is no,” Jen King, a privacy researcher at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence told WaPo . “You can’t be sure that it’ll be totally private.”

And though users are remarkably comfortable divulging those details to their favorite bot, fewer are aware of those myriad ways their chat logs might live on in perpetuity. According to the DuckDuckGo poll, 53 percent of regular users said they didn’t know that AI chatbots are training on data obtained through their conversation, while 75 percent didn’t realize that conversations with large language models (LLMs) can easily be subpoenaed by police.

So when in doubt about whether to tell ChatGPT about your intimate relationship troubles , keep in mind that the internet is forever; and that goes double for AI chatbots.

The tech world’s potential future founders are living out hedonistic existences in giant Silicon Valley mansions, where they live with a dozen and even more like-minded individuals, and where life is more a less a constant party. These so-called hacker houses, though, have a dark side.

A recent New York Times investigation has uncovered several harassment cases and rape allegations stemming from hacker houses. The most prominent of these is the AGI House — short for “artificial general intelligence” — in Hillsborough, where police have logged 37 incidents since 2022. At least 17 were related to the often large and extravagant parties and events that were regularly being thrown on the property.

In December, a woman called the Hillsborough police station at 2 in the morning from a Lyft, reporting that she had been trapped at the AGI House by a male resident who tried to force her to have sex.

The man told her she was old and “would be alone forever,” according to the police reported viewed by the NYT . He was “persistent in attempting to convince” the woman “to have sex with him, and she repeatedly declined.”

She escaped by climbing over a gate, unharmed.

The AGI House was founded by Jeremy Nixon, a former Google researcher who’s established other tech homes, with the vision of having “20 AI hackers, living in the same epic house for three months,” he told the NYT . The domicile was originally called NeoGenesis, but rebranded after OpenAI released ChatGPT and kickstarted the AI boom. And before NeoGenesis, he co-founded a hacker house called Genesis in 2019.

Genesis had a dark history of its own. Not wanting for debauchery, it was also a hub for parties, with one 19-year-old tech entrepreneur claiming he used to sneak into parties when he was just 13. “It was pretty crazy,” he told the NYT .

Yehong Zhu, 30, filed a police reporting accusing a former Genesis house member of rape and assault in December 2021. Zhu has lived in four tech houses, and her view of them as utopic spaces for entrepreneurs was shattered by her experience. The case is still under investigation, and the accused Genesis resident hasn’t left the house and can’t be located, she said.

“I’m far from the only one this has happened to,” Zhu, who founded her own startup called Zette AI, told the NYT .

To lay out the stakes, these hacker houses aren’t random gatherings. Some are directly run by tech executives like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has advised one called the Residency. AGI House regularly had tech industry royalty show up for dinners, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin. In a direct way, they’re responsible for fostering the culture and beliefs that the current and upcoming generations of AI industry workers, if not leaders, are being instilled with, along with building the network of connections that’ll shape their careers. The next Sam Altman or Elon Musk is probably spending their formative young adult years in one of these debaucherous dens.

The people running them are well aware of their outsized influence. The AGI House’s current manager, venture capitalist Rocky Yu, is in an ongoing legal battle with a former manager over who owns the rights to the AGI House brand, the NYT noted.

There’re other signs that all is not well behind closed doors. Police were also asked to perform welfare checks on at least four different occasions at the AGI House. On one occasion, they even sent an ambulance to the house.

So far, the long-fear AI job-apocalypse has been little more than smoke and mirrors, with one gigantic exception: entry-level tech workers.

According to a new report on New York City jobs data compiled by the nonprofit Center for an Urban Future — first reported by the City — job postings for entry-level roles in “computer and mathematical” occupations has plummeted by 49 percent since 2022, the latest indication that tech firms are using AI to justify a massive slowdown in new hires.

Though computer science grads are bearing the brunt of the mayhem, tech jobs may just be the first domino to fall. As Urban Future’s executive director Jon Bowles told the City , “entry-level postings” overall have “fallen off a cliff, and the first rung of the ladder in tech is under pressure.”

“For many years, these were amazing opportunities for people getting a job because tech was growing so fast and adding so many entry-level jobs,” Bowles continued. “Those positions for young people with limited experience are harder to come by and there is intense competition.”

Other industries with drastically lower entry-level hiring include roles in office and administrative support; financial operations; arts, design, entertainment, sports, and media; and roles in education and libraries, among others.

While AI is the most obvious variable at play here, there are many other factors helping contribute to a decline in entry-level job postings. For one thing, tech companies have been slashing jobs left and right to reverse COVID-era overhiring, coinciding with the rise of generative AI.

The Urban Future findings also come amidst a rapidly decaying job market in the US, with nearly a quarter of the US labor force functionally unemployed as of July.

All told, AI certainly isn’t improving things, but if we were to shut down every AI chatbot tomorrow, it’s highly unlikely that entry level jobs would rebound on their own.

A new paper published in the Journal of the American Medical Association this month concluded, after surveying hundreds of studies on AI in medicine, that not only is AI already an indispensable tool that supports doctors, but that it’s in many ways surpassing them, and will soon be able to care patients on its own better than a human physician could.

“In cognitive medical functions, AI-alone medical care is likely to be better than physician-only or physician-AI hybrid care,” the authors, the widely renowned bioethicist Ezekiel Emanuel and venture capitalist Vinod Khosla, flatly declare.

But many physicians aren’t having it, Wired reports . One of the paper’s chief critics is the CEO of the American Medical Association himself, John Whyte. According to Whyte, some of the studies it surveyed are simulations, instead of blinded experiments, the gold standard of medical studies. And some contradict the author’s conclusions, such as a Nature article from February that found that most patients had a hard time talking to AI chatbots to get the expertise they needed, he argued.

“The AMA does see the potential in these tools, but they have to be utilized in the context of a care plan that’s governed by a physician,” Whyte told Wired .

The controversial study cites the rapid progress of LLMs since being publicly introduced in November 2022 with the release of ChatGPT. In spite of the tech’s relatively young age, the paper claims it already surpasses doctors at five fundamental tasks, which include: eliciting relevant medical information from patients, diagnosing the patient and conducting diagnostic testing, and managing chronic diseases.

This gap between physicians and AI will widen because AI is “rapidly improving,” it predicts, while human doctors have their own capabilities diminished, or are “deskilled,” by becoming dependent on the very same AI models.

“We’re making a prediction for four years from now,” Emanuel told Wired . “You don’t think that [AI is] going to be way more advanced than a doctor?”

Taking this to its logical endpoint, the paper makes another bold claim: human physicians are better off not getting in AI’s way, finding that human-AI hybrids “actually degrade performance compared with AI alone.”

“Thus, as AI improves, having humans in the loop will likely worsen patient care,” it adds.

There’s a kernel of truth to this. AI-deskilling is already happening, with senior doctors warning of how med students are already heavily relying on AI tools. To be fair to the med students, though, so are actual doctors: internal data from OpenEvidence , an AI chatbot specifically designed for clinicians, suggests that around two thirds of physicians in the US are using the tool.

New ground in AI in medical applications, meanwhile, is being broken seemingly every day. Last week, a team of neurosurgeons in the UK announced that they’d used an AI tool that guided them as they performed surgery to remove a tumor from a patient’s brain.

Robert Wachter, head of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco (and a friend of Emanuel), cautions that AI and humans together are better for now, but that in the future, there “will be times when humans will muck up the performance,” he told Wired .

Still, he emphasized that human doctors will always be irreplaceable. He called the idea of AI automating doctor’s jobs an example of the “doorman fallacy”: the fear that doormen would be made obsolete with the introduction of automatic doors. Doormen stuck around, accepting packages while also providing an air of hospitality that a robotic door can’t. The idea that highly trained doctors who spend years of their life honing their craft will become a bougie novelty like the doorman, somehow, is meant to be comforting.

In any case, it’s common to hear highfalutin claims to come from advocates of AI technology, and nearly as common to see holes poked in them. Advocates of AI in education declared victory when a much-hyped study concluded that ChatGPT can have a “large positive impact on improving learning performance,” for instance, but the study was later retracted by the publisher Springer Nature after it found major discrepancies in its analysis.

Content warning: this story contains descriptions of disturbing AI-generated videos that depict violent child abuse.

As Meta has embraced AI at a deep corporate level over the past few years, its users’ feeds on Facebook and Instagram have been overrun with AI-generated material.

Much of this AI content is insipid or manipulative , clearly produced at scale to take advantage of Meta’s indifference to the slop by harvesting as many human eyeballs as possible in various monetization schemes.

Some of the AI material has now grown so dark that it defies easy comprehension. A Futurism investigation has uncovered a huge number of Facebook accounts uploading streams of videos depicting violent child abuse — and Meta is barely pretending to care about taking them down.

Facebook accounts dedicated to the horrific content have uploaded videos of babies and young children being slapped, kicked, bludgeoned with heavy objects, dragged by their hair, burned with stoves and irons, chained up and locked in cages and freezers, thrown down stairs, threatened with knives and guns, starved, made to eat dog food and garbage off the floor, and much more.

In one video, a woman screams at a little girl to stop crying.

“Please don’t hit Noah, hit me instead,” the girl sobs, with cuts and bruises on her cheek and forehead, as another child cowers.

In another, a visibly dirty boy begs for food.

“Please ma’am, just a few dollars for food,” he implores a woman, prompting her to slap him in the face twice. He falls to the floor, bleeding from his nose.

In another, a man drips wax from a burning candle onto the hands of a boy who has been tied up.

“It hurts!” the boy cries, flinching in pain.

Some of the cruelties in the videos are astonishing in their specificity, seemingly generated at scale using repeated prompts. Some involve withholding an inhaler from a child who needs it, while others show allergic children forced to eat shellfish. Others show adults pouring snakes and cockroaches on weeping kids. One video shows a woman throwing a baby into a fire pit. Many more involve young Black children being whipped or beaten by white adults as they perform manual labor in what looks like a colonial African setting.

The videos aren’t quite photorealistic, but they are clearly being generated with cutting-edge technology, and the effect is distressing. Many commenters on the videos, which often attract thousands or even tens of thousands of reactions on Facebook, seem unaware that they’re synthetic, with many reacting in horror — or begging for a follow-up video that continues the disturbing narrative.

“You psycho, why are you abusing the child,” wrote one user on a video of a woman slapping a boy in the face with a belt, leaving a bloody mark around his eye. “You deserve a punishment and a big one.”

At first, we thought that we could map out the full network of accounts sharing the child abuse content. But after days of reviewing accounts and videos, we kept finding hundreds more. In effect, the supply seems to be endless, with the creators of the material uploading it as fast as we could identify it.

Meta’s policy about violence against children is phrased ambiguously, saying that it bans “videos or photos that depict real or non-real non-sexual child abuse regardless of sharing intent, unless the imagery is from real-world art, cartoons, movies or video games.” The policy doesn’t clarify whether those carve-outs include AI-generated content.

Contacted with questions and examples of the sickening videos, Meta offered a brief statement.

“We have strict rules against content that depicts physical harm to children — whether it’s real or AI-generated — and we have removed these videos,” it read.

Meta has long struggled to control the proliferation of troubling content on its platforms. Just this week, Wired reported that the company has accepted money from advertisers to run hundreds of promos for “nudify” apps that contained AI-generated sexual imagery of children, including numerous real-life minors whose photos were pilfered from social media and stock images.

Provided with numerous examples of the violent child abuse content and asked whether Meta would work to proactively take the material down, the company’s spokesperson declined to comment on the record, opting only to share a Meta page about the company’s efforts to automatically remove child abuse content. The data on the page is hard to parse and doesn’t specify how many videos of violent child abuse the company removes, never mind whether they’re AI-generated.

One defense the Meta spokesperson offered is that many of the videos first show violence against children before an adult steps in to protect the child. This is trivially true in many examples, but it feels more like a proactive defense by the creators of the content against attempts at moderation, or perhaps a strategy to evade guardrails on an AI video generator. And in reality, the mass-produced videos sometimes devolve into orgies of brutality in which the violence against children gives way to various adults punching and slapping each other in ways that don’t make sense.

The company removed the majority of the videos we flagged to its press team, but left others online. The videos it opted not to remove included one depicting a young girl shut in a chest freezer, another showing a boy discarded in a trash can where he is seen gnawing on bones, and another of a girl in a classroom environment being forced to eat garbage.

Curious about how Meta polices such vile content in practice, we conducted a test by reporting eight accounts that had been sharing AI-generated child abuse videos.

Out of the eight accounts we reported, Meta eventually removed only two — and in one of those cases, it initially rejected the report before overriding the decision and taking it down. The timelines for action were lengthy, exceeding a week.

“We’ve taken a look and found that the page doesn’t go against our Community Standards,” the company wrote.

The six accounts that the company’s moderators left up had shared many heinous videos, including a toddler being struck in the face with a frying pan, a girl being beaten with a baseball bat, and a baby being kicked. (After a thoughtful internal discussion, we are opting not to share any of the videos at this time; if you are a member of the media considering follow-up coverage, please feel free to email us and we can provide examples to corroborate our reporting.)

If Meta were serious about proactively taking down the child abuse content, or detecting it at the time of upload, it would almost certainly be able to do so.

In fact, AI systems could probably be helpful: the company has invested hundreds of billions of dollars toward building “superintelligence” — reportedly making offers to top talent in the industry that have exceeded a billion dollars for a single hire — with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg saying last year that “whoever gets there first is going to have a long-term, durable advantage towards building one of the most important products in history.”

The tech to moderate these types of videos automatically already exists. In rudimentary testing, we found that Anthropic’s Claude AI was adept at evaluating whether videos contain imagery of violence against children.

For that matter, Meta appears to have already deployed systems that can identify the stomach-turning videos, even if it’s declining to use them to moderate content on its platforms. We identified the vast majority of the horrid accounts simply by loading one of them, and then scrolling Facebook’s recommendation feature, which eagerly provided a bottomless feed of similar appalling material.

In other words, Meta has extraordinary resources at its disposal to remove the child abuse videos, or to prevent them from being uploaded in the first place. But even when the material is flagged to it directly by journalists or reported by concerned users, it’s dragging its feet and refusing to delete it — a familiar pattern for a company that has long claimed to care about abuses of its platforms while doing little to stop them .

When we presented that line of thinking to Meta, the final abhorrent videos we’d flagged to the company’s press team finally disappeared from Facebook — though untold thousands remain on its platforms.

The company also provided a brief final statement.

“Not all the links you sent violate our policies,” it read. “Can you please avoid suggesting in your reporting that they do?”

“They’re flat, the styling is mediocre and the images are too ‘perfect’ in a bad way,” Oberg continued. “The models look dead in the eyes and don’t have any organic movement whatsoever. The images are empty and void of any feeling or emotion.”

Oberg chalked up the AI’s failure to the reality that taste is “felt, not learned.” And image-generating AI models are, after all, learning models; they don’t have lived experiences that translate into a particular way of viewing the world around them and the objects within it, nor do they have a certain “ je ne sais quoi .” Though taste is a way through which people communicate with each other, taste itself is something that’s often unexplainable.

“The smartest AI in the world can learn everything there is to know about taste and style,” she added, “but the feeling will never be there.”

People “who truly have good taste don’t follow trends, they set them,” wrote Oberg. “More than this, they set them without trying to, it happens by just being themselves and liking what they like, not because an algorithm or AI told them to.”

A key question that remains is whether other brands will continue to view a human touch worth it for the cost — or if they’ll charge ahead with AI nonetheless .

It’s a thorny topic as lawmakers ponder whether to intervene as companies are increasingly using AI tools to analyze consumers’ personal data to tailor price tags in real time, a controversial practice called “surveillance pricing.” While Productrise’s experiment doesn’t necessarily prove that Google is discriminating on price by using the wealth of data it has on users, the discrepancy raises plenty of questions over how AI Mode arrives at its recommendations — and why prices appear to differ compared to regular search.

“While we haven’t verified the accuracy of the claims in this report, all shopping results on Google Search, including AI Mode and the search results page, are powered by the same data source: our Shopping Graph,” Google told us. “Shoppers can easily click into a product listing to compare prices for that product across retailers and choose the best option for them.”

Beyond showing a higher price for the same exact product, the study also found that AI Mode listings are far more visible to users, sitting “49 percent higher than traditional search listings.” The primary vendor for the same exact product differed just under 50 percent of the time between the two modes, suggesting AI Mode is prioritizing a strikingly different — and less budget-oriented — group of sellers.

“This is a fascinating study that reveals more about Google’s Shopping Graph and the inconsistencies between classic search and AI Mode for free listing placements,” said independent SEO consultant Brodie Clark in a statement shared by Productrise.

However, whether consumers are actually willing to pay those higher prices is a different matter. Many, the research found, are clicking past the AI feature to find the actual best value.

“While the higher price might be displayed within the grid result in AI Mode (making the top-level comparison less accurate), what we tend to see is that the retailer with the lowest price gets the click in the end,” Clark explained.

That controversy is still rippling through the math world. But what has the AI’s solution taught us? Not a lot, as it turns out, because the proof it wrote, while technically correct, is borderline incomprehensible.

“So far it’s been very difficult to really extract any human understanding from this new AI proof,” James Maynard, an Oxford mathematician, told NPR .

“The paper is not written for humans,” echoed Javier Gómez-Serrano, a mathematician at Brown University who uses AI in his own research. The AI’s proof could help the field after “some serious re-writing,” he added, but “as of today, the paper doesn’t teach us much.”

The Navier-Stokes equations mathematically describe how fluids, ranging from a rush of wind to the churn of ocean currents, move and behave. They’ve been used for nearly two centuries with reliable results, but why they work remains something of a mystery. Scientists have been eager to push the equations to their limits and see if their predictions could reach a breaking point where they describe a scenario that makes no sense in the real world. Reifying the equation’s importance, the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000 listed the Navier-Stokes as one of its six Millennium Problems, with the prize for solving it at $1 million.

OpenAI claimed that its swarm of AI agents identified a scenario in which the fluids accelerate to an infinite velocity, creating a “blow up” or singularity — something, of course, that’s impossible in the physical universe.

Hours before the announcement, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, who had been working on the Navier-Stokes problem for years, accused OpenAI of jumping on his work without notice or permission, and thereby essentially pilfering his ideas by pushing them over the finish line. He claimed that OpenAI’s work followed a similar path to his own, which he says that no one else in the field was pursuing. Because he’d been using OpenAI’s Codex tool to help with his research , he insinuated, OpenAI may have secretly accessed his notes. When he approached OpenAI about this, he claims that the company said it would credit him on its paper if he dropped his collaborator, Levent Alpöge, who was working at Anthropic.

OpenAI denied the allegations but admitted that it “cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.”

There’s also some groaning about the Navier-Stokes problem OpenAI says it solved. To earn the Clay Institute’s Millennium prize, mathematicians could solve either the “forced” or “unforced” version of the problem. The forced version involved an external force like gravity applied to the fluids. As laid out in a recent Scientific American piece , experts are chiefly interested in finding a purer scenario where the equations “blow up” without an external force and only with the forces within the fluid. OpenAI’s solution, however, relies on an external force. More than that, a recent proof posted by mathematicians contends that OpenAI’s solution can never lead to solving the full problem.

“The most important problem is unsolved,” Luis Silvestre, a mathematician at the University of Chicago, told SciAm . “The Clay problem is settled, but the main problem for the Navier-Stokes equations is not.”

Still, mathematicians are in agreement that, however technical it may be, OpenAI’s solutions are valid, even if it’ll take many more weeks to unpack the AI’s ramblings.

In the age of AI agents, it’s no longer enough to ask how much electricity a single chatbot prompt uses. Today’s AI models are even more complicated systems, often designed to complete complex tasks autonomously, and are made up not only of large language models, but a host of other tools and application layers which demand much more power than the humble standalone chatbot.

That makes calculating their total electricity usage a much bigger can of worms. Yet with virtual radio silence from the top private AI labs on internal energy use, it’s nearly impossible to say definitively what kind of impact our AI assistants are having on the electrical grid.

In a blog post flagged by Wired ‘s Molly Taft, the climate scientist Zeke Hausfather took it upon himself to calculate the likely energy demand behind his typical sessions with Claude Code, an AI-coding assistant developed by Anthropic.

Measuring the number of tokens his AI assistant consumed, Hausfather estimated that his average daily use fell in the range of 1.2 to 5.9 kWh — an alarming amount for a single consumer, consuming more electricity than two refrigerators running all day long.

Most of this token consumption, 3.2 billion over an eight-week period, came from the agent “re-reading its own working memory,” Hausfather wrote, which happens every time the tool takes a new step.

“Every time an agent takes a step (eg, runs a command, reads a file, or calls a tool), the model re-processes its entire accumulated context,” the climate scientist wrote.

“The text I actually see (eg, the model’s output) is only around 0.4 percent of total tokens processed,” Hausfather continued. “Some 96 percent of the tokens are cache reads where the agent re-reads its own context at each of those 14,000 steps. This matters enormously for the energy estimate, because a cached token is much cheaper to re-read than a fresh one is to process.”

Extrapolating those results out over a year, Hausfather contends that he would emit “a bit more per year than running an electric clothes dryer, and about half as much as driving an electric car 11,500 miles in California.”

That might not sound like much, but over an entire population of AI users, it adds up quickly. Likewise, it “represents a net new source of emissions, at a time when global temperatures are skyrocketing and our emissions reduction goals are increasingly off track,” the climate scientist explains.

The exact climate toll, though, remains hazy. As Wired notes, AI sustainability researcher Boris Gamazaychikov called the calculation a “good effort,” but one based on old data. Gamazaychikov’s own research on agentic AI energy consumption should be due out later in September — and when it drops, it could drastically change our understanding of the true cost of AI agents.

The low-rent beat alone should be a dead giveaway. And while AI music generating tools certainly have come a long way, giving the fake Mathers a passing imitation of the real one’s voice and delivery, the plasticky sound of the vocals make it clear that it’s not the real deal.

Nonetheless, users on YouTube were fooled hook, line, and sinker.

“This is fire eminem is the goat hands down,” one user gushed.

“Really Proud of you Eminem!!” another wrote. “You really are getting it and not giving up!! Keep going!”

The video’s title gives no indication that it’s not a real release, and doesn’t feature YouTube’s official AI label. Buried in its description is a strangely-phrased disclaimer.

“Fan-made music videos inspired by Eminem, Slim Shady, and legendary Detroit hip-hop,” it reads. “This is a fan-made audiovisual project created for entertainment purposes only.”

The owner of the account even proactively offers up an email address for “copyright concerns or removal requests,” suggesting they’re all too familiar with the process of having angry record labels try to shut them down or get hung up in YouTube’s infamous copyright filters.

A web search for the email address reveals that it’s also listed on a litany of other YouTube accounts, many of which masquerade as other rap artists, including Meek Mill — an account that has over 13,000 subscribers — and 21 Savage .

Some of the tracks have been affixed with an “AI” label by YouTube , indicating that “sounds or visuals were altered or fully generated.”

Reached by email, the account owner offered their thoughts on the situation.

“No, my intention was never to make it look like a genuine new Eminem release,” the creator, who goes by the name Milana Salaeva, told Futurism in a message, referring to the “I’m Back” track. “I make it clear in the description that the content is unofficial and that AI-generated or AI-assisted elements may be used.”

“I’m a music producer, and I’ve been making music myself for quite some time,” they added. “I often create my own beats and handle the arrangement, mixing, mastering, and other parts of the production process. AI is just one of the tools I sometimes use as part of that workflow.”

The Eminem mimicry is only a drop in a bucket in an internet dominated by AI-generated music. The space publication Space Daily , which has been operating for over three decades, has become an unrecognizable shell of its former self after a company called Brown Brothers Media bought it and turned it into a content mill that pumps out misleading and badly sourced AI slop.

As a Futurism investigation found, Space Daily is averaging an estimated ten million page views per month. That would be an incredible success story — if it weren’t for the fact that it’s been platforming non-existent experts as puppets to churn out AI garbage.

Case in point, one of the website’s authors, “Dr. Katherine Chen,” was identified as a former “systems engineer” at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory who “spent fifteen years designing autonomous systems for deep space missions,” according to her since-deleted profile on the site.

A different writer, listed as “Dr. James Whitfield” by Space Daily , was allegedly an “aerospace medicine researcher at the European Space Agency.”

But Futurism confirmed that neither Chen nor Whitfield actually exist. Instead, Brown Brothers Media invented their personas to publish slop on a massive scale under the bylines of what looked like trustworthy experts.

“Mr. James Whitfield is not currently employed by the European Space Agency, nor do our records indicate that he has ever worked here in the past,” the ESA told us in a statement. While NASA declined to comment, its website doesn’t make a single mention of a “Katherine Chen.”

After we started investigating Brown Brothers Media, the company began mass-deleting vast numbers of articles. It also deleted many of the fake writers, including Chen and Whitfield.

“Before May 2026, our publications used contributor bylines that did not identify real people, and some of those biographies included credentials that were not real,” the company conceded in a statement. “That was wrong. In May, we stopped publishing under those bylines, began removing or correcting the older articles involved, and published network-wide and per-site editorial standards. That review is ongoing.”

After the mass culling, Space Daily is still publishing plenty of articles, albeit under shadowy bylines like “Space Daily Editorial Team,” or “Mission Notes.” Many of the articles claim to have been edited by either one of the Brown Brothers Media founders, a member of its editorial team, or a constellation of contributors.

Its subsequent output hasn’t been inspiring. Its homepage prominently featured an awkwardly-written piece about an encounter between the ESA’s Rosetta spacecraft and Comet 67P — which happened over a decade ago . The only reason Space Daily is talking about it now, obviously, is to get clicks by flooding the zone in an attempt to trick Google’s algorithms.

Even a brief perusal of the content being published raises red flags. A piece with the brain-meltingly long headline “A Trillion-Mile Stream of Gas Is Falling Onto a Triple Star, and It Lines Up With the Outermost of Its Three Tilted Rings to Within Three Degrees” is virtually incomprehensible, taking the form of a jumble of words about “angles,” “fitted numbers,” and “misalignments.” (Pangram found it to be entirely AI-generated, with no sign of human editing.)

The article is bylined by Chris Jeremia, who appears to be a “meat proxy,” or an individual Brown Brothers Media uses by affixing their name to a fully AI-generated piece. Besides publishing articles about astrophysics and cuneiform clay tablets , Jeremia also is listed as the magazine editor of VegOut , and also finds time to cover beluga whales in Canada that face euthanasia for The Vessel — both other AI content mills run by Brown Brothers Media.

She may exist in the real world, but Jeremia appears to have just as much editorial authority as Dr. Chen and Dr. Whitfield.
